content: Thyroid hormone should never be used as a treatment for obesity in individuals with normal thyroid function. It is not effective for weight loss in such cases and can lead to severe or even life-threatening toxicity, particularly when combined with amphetamines like benzphetamine, dextroamphetamine, or methamphetamine. Discuss the potential risks of this medication with your doctor. Thyroid hormone is a naturally occurring substance produced by the body. When prescribed, it is used to manage symptoms of hypothyroidism, a condition in which the thyroid gland does not produce sufficient thyroid hormone. Symptoms of hypothyroidism include fatigue, depression, constipation, weight gain, hair loss, dry skin, coarse hair, muscle cramps, difficulty concentrating, generalized aches and pains, leg swelling, and increased sensitivity to cold. Thyroid medication is also used to treat goiter, which is an enlargement of the thyroid gland. This medication belongs to a class of drugs known as thyroid agents and works by supplementing the thyroid hormone that the body is unable to produce adequately. Thyroid medication is available in tablet form and is taken orally, typically once daily before breakfast. It is important to take the medication at the same time each day. Follow the instructions on your prescription label carefully, and consult your doctor or pharmacist if you have any questions. Take the medication exactly as prescribed, without altering the dose or frequency. Your doctor will likely start you on a low dose and gradually increase it. While thyroid medication helps manage the symptoms of hypothyroidism, it does not cure the condition. It may take several weeks before you notice an improvement in your symptoms. Most patients with hypothyroidism will need to take this medication for the rest of their lives. Continue taking the medication even if you feel well, and do not stop without consulting your doctor. This medication may also be prescribed for other purposes. Consult your doctor or pharmacist for additional information. Before starting thyroid medication, inform your doctor and pharmacist if you are allergic to thyroid, any other medications, pork, or any of the ingredients in the tablets. Request a list of ingredients from your pharmacist if needed. Provide a complete list of all prescription and nonprescription medications, vitamins, and supplements you are currently taking or plan to take.g., danazol, testosterone), anticoagulants (e.g., warfarin), antidepressants, aprepitant, carbamazepine, diabetes medications, digoxin, efavirenz, estrogen, griseofulvin, human growth hormone, insulin, lovastatin, nevirapine, oral contraceptives containing estrogen, oral steroids (e.g., dexamethasone, methylprednisolone, prednisone), phenobarbital, phenytoin, potassium iodide, rifabutin, rifampin, ritonavir, salicylate pain relievers (e.g., aspirin, choline magnesium trisalicylate, diflunisal, magnesium salicylate, salsalate), strong iodine solution, and theophylline. If you take cholestyramine or colestipol, take them at least four hours before your thyroid medication. Similarly, if you take antacids, iron-containing supplements, simethicone, or sucralfate, take them at least four hours before or after your thyroid medication. Inform your doctor if you use herbal products, particularly St. John’s wort. Notify your doctor if you have a history of diabetes, osteoporosis, atherosclerosis, cardiovascular conditions (e.g. If you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding, inform your doctor. If you become pregnant while taking thyroid medication, contact your doctor immediately. If you are scheduled for surgery, including dental procedures, inform your healthcare provider that you are taking thyroid medication. Unless otherwise directed by your doctor, you may continue your normal diet while taking this medication. If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. However, if it is close to the time of your next dose, skip the missed dose and resume your regular schedule. Do not take a double dose to compensate for a missed one. Inform your doctor if you miss two or more consecutive doses. Thyroid medication may cause side effects. Notify your doctor if any of the following symptoms are severe or persistent: weight loss, uncontrollable shaking, headache, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, stomach cramps, hyperactivity, anxiety, irritability, difficulty sleeping, flushing, increased appetite, fever, changes in menstrual cycle, muscle weakness, or temporary hair loss (especially in children during the first month of treatment). Some side effects can be serious. Contact your doctor immediately if you experience any of the following: rash, difficulty breathing or swallowing, chest pain, rapid or irregular heartbeat, swelling of the hands, feet, ankles, or lower legs, excessive sweating, heat intolerance, nervousness, or seizures. Report any unusual symptoms to your doctor. Serious side effects can also be reported to the FDA’s MedWatch Adverse Event Reporting program. Store this medication in its original container, tightly sealed, and out of reach of children. Keep it at room temperature, away from excessive heat and moisture. Do not store it in the bathroom. Dispose of expired or unused medication properly, and consult your pharmacist for guidance on disposal. In case of overdose, contact your local poison control center at 1-800-222-1222. If the individual has collapsed or is not breathing, call 911 immediately. Keep all appointments with your doctor and laboratory. Your doctor will order tests to monitor your response to the medication. Inform laboratory personnel that you are taking thyroid medication before undergoing any tests. Thyroid tablets may have a strong odor, but this does not indicate spoilage or ineffectiveness. Learn both the brand and generic names of your medication, and verify your prescription each time it is refilled. Do not switch brands without consulting your doctor or pharmacist, as different brands may contain slightly varying amounts of the active ingredient. Do not share your medication with others. Consult your pharmacist if you have questions about refilling your prescription. Brand names for this medication include Armour® Thyroid. Other names include dessicated thyroid, thyroid extract, and thyroid gland.
